name: hydrogen
funFact: The most abundant element in the universe — roughly 74% of all normal matter.

name: oxygen
funFact: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and is magnetic — it sticks between the poles of a magnet.

name: nitrogen
funFact: The triple bond in N2 is one of the strongest in chemistry — 941 kJ/mol.

name: chlorine
funFact: A yellow-green gas that was used as a chemical weapon in 1915.

name: fluorine
funFact: The most electronegative element — it attacks nearly everything, even glass.

name: bromine
funFact: One of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.

name: iodine
funFact: Sublimes directly from black crystals to a violet vapour.

name: water
funFact: Ice floats because hydrogen bonding holds water molecules further apart in the solid than in the liquid.

name: hydrogen peroxide
funFact: Its skewed 'open book' shape is what makes it such a reactive oxidiser.

name: carbon monoxide
funFact: Binds haemoglobin 200× more strongly than oxygen does — that is why it kills silently.

name: carbon dioxide
funFact: Symmetric, so despite two polar C=O bonds the molecule has zero net dipole.

name: ammonia
funFact: The Haber process that makes it feeds roughly half of the world's population.

name: methane
funFact: Methane is 28× more potent than CO2 as a greenhouse gas over 100 years.

name: hydrogen chloride
funFact: Dissolved in water it becomes hydrochloric acid — the same acid in your stomach.

name: hydrogen fluoride
funFact: Uniquely, it attacks glass — so it must be stored in plastic bottles.

name: hydrogen sulfide
funFact: Smells of rotten eggs at 0.5 ppb — then paralyses your sense of smell above 100 ppm.

name: sulfur dioxide
funFact: The cause of acid rain — it oxidises to SO3 and then to H2SO4 in the atmosphere.

name: sulfur trioxide
funFact: Reacting it directly with water creates an uncontrollable acid mist — industry dissolves it in H2SO4 instead.

name: sulfuric acid
funFact: More of it is made than any other chemical on Earth — about 250 million tonnes a year.

name: nitric acid
funFact: Known to alchemists as aqua fortis — it dissolves every metal except gold and platinum.

name: phosphoric acid
funFact: The tangy note in cola — about 0.05% by mass.

name: carbonic acid
funFact: Your blood uses the carbonic-acid/bicarbonate pair to hold pH at 7.4.

name: sodium chloride
funFact: A 1 cm cube of salt contains about 2.2 × 10²² ions.

name: magnesium oxide
funFact: It melts at 2852 °C, which is why it lines steel furnaces.

name: calcium oxide
funFact: Known as quicklime; slaking it with water releases enough heat to boil the water.

name: calcium carbonate
funFact: Chalk, marble, limestone, eggshells and coral are all the same compound.

name: aluminium oxide
funFact: Ruby and sapphire are aluminium oxide with chromium or iron impurities.

name: sodium hydroxide
funFact: Called caustic soda; dissolving it in water is dramatically exothermic.

name: sodium bicarbonate
funFact: Baking soda releases CO2 above 80 °C — that is what makes cakes rise.

name: silicon dioxide
funFact: Quartz, sand and opal are all SiO2 — the most abundant compound in Earth's crust.

name: silicon carbide
funFact: Nearly as hard as diamond and used as a moissanite gemstone.

name: iron(III) oxide
funFact: Thermite — Fe2O3 plus aluminium — burns hot enough to melt steel.

name: copper(II) sulfate
funFact: Anhydrous CuSO4 is white — it turns blue the instant it meets water.

name: silver chloride
funFact: Darkens in sunlight because light reduces Ag⁺ to metallic silver — the basis of film photography.

name: potassium permanganate
funFact: Its intense purple comes from charge transfer, not from a d–d transition.

name: boron trifluoride
funFact: Electron deficient with only six electrons on boron — a classic Lewis acid.

name: beryllium chloride
funFact: Linear in the gas phase — the textbook example of sp hybridisation with only four electrons on the central atom.

name: diborane
funFact: Contains two three-centre two-electron 'banana' bonds — it broke the classical valence model.

name: phosphorus pentachloride
funFact: In the solid it is actually [PCl4]⁺[PCl6]⁻ — the 'molecular' form only exists as a gas.

name: sulfur tetrafluoride
funFact: The classic see-saw shape: one equatorial lone pair on a trigonal bipyramid.

name: sulfur hexafluoride
funFact: 23 500× worse than CO2 as a greenhouse gas, and so dense you can 'float' a boat on it.

name: xenon difluoride
funFact: The first noble gas compound made by simply heating xenon and fluorine together.

name: xenon tetrafluoride
funFact: Two lone pairs sit trans to each other — the textbook square-planar AX4E2 case.

name: chlorine trifluoride
funFact: It sets fire to glass, concrete and asbestos — and has burned through a metre of concrete in an industrial spill.

name: bromine pentafluoride
funFact: Square pyramidal AX5E1 — the one lone pair pushes the four basal fluorines down.

name: iodine heptafluoride
funFact: One of very few molecules with a pentagonal bipyramidal shape.

name: ozone
funFact: Smells sharp after thunderstorms — the word comes from the Greek ozein, 'to smell'.

name: nitrous oxide
funFact: Laughing gas — also 273× worse than CO2 as a greenhouse gas.

name: nitric oxide
funFact: A free radical that is also a neurotransmitter — it relaxes blood vessels.

name: nitrogen dioxide
funFact: The reddish-brown colour of city smog.

name: hydrogen cyanide
funFact: Smells of bitter almonds — but 40% of people cannot smell it at all.

name: silicon tetrachloride
funFact: Used to make military smoke screens — the HCl it releases pulls water from the air into a dense fog.

name: tetrachloromethane
funFact: Symmetric, so it is non-polar — yet it dissolves grease superbly.

name: phosgene
funFact: Used as a chemical weapon in WWI; today tonnes of it feed the plastics industry.

name: methanol
funFact: Called wood alcohol — it was once made by distilling wood, and it blinds you.

name: ethanol
funFact: The oldest recreational drug — residue in 9000-year-old Chinese pottery proves it.

name: ethane-1,2-diol
funFact: Sweet-tasting and lethal — the body oxidises it to oxalic acid.

name: glycerol
funFact: Nitrating it gives nitroglycerin — the same molecule that is both heart medicine and dynamite.

name: formaldehyde
funFact: The simplest aldehyde — and the reason biology labs smell so distinctive.

name: acetaldehyde
funFact: Your liver makes it from alcohol — its build-up is what causes a hangover.

name: acetone
funFact: Your body makes acetone when it burns fat instead of sugar — that is the 'ketone breath' of fasting.

name: formic acid
funFact: Named after ants (formica) — it is what makes an ant bite sting.

name: acetic acid
funFact: Pure acetic acid freezes at 16.6 °C — lab bottles of it crystallise and are called 'glacial'.

name: butanoic acid
funFact: The smell of rancid butter and vomit.

name: ethane
funFact: Second-largest component of natural gas; cracking it gives the ethylene that becomes most plastics.

name: ethene
funFact: The most produced organic compound on Earth — about 150 million tonnes a year.

name: ethyne
funFact: Burning it with pure oxygen reaches 3300 °C — hot enough to cut steel.

name: buta-1,3-diene
funFact: All four carbons are sp² and the π system is delocalised — conjugation is why it is so reactive.

name: cyclopropane
funFact: Its C–C–C angles are forced to 60° instead of 109.5° — enormous angle strain.

name: cyclohexane
funFact: Sits in a 'chair', not a flat hexagon — that is what keeps every angle near 109.5°.

name: benzene
funFact: Kekulé claimed the ring came to him in a dream of a snake biting its own tail.

name: toluene
funFact: Toluene + nitric acid ×3 = TNT.

name: phenol
funFact: Joseph Lister sprayed it over surgical wounds in 1865 — the birth of antiseptic surgery.

name: aniline
funFact: The first synthetic dye, mauveine, was made by accident from aniline in 1856.

name: naphthalene
funFact: Two fused benzene rings — 10 π electrons, still aromatic (4n+2 with n=2).

name: diethyl ether
funFact: Publicly demonstrated as an anaesthetic in 1846 — surgery never went back.

name: ethyl acetate
funFact: The smell of pear drops — esters are responsible for most fruit aromas.

name: octane
funFact: The '100' on the petrol pump is iso-octane — 2,2,4-trimethylpentane.

name: ethanethiol
funFact: Added to natural gas so you can smell a leak — detectable at 1 part per billion.

name: urea
funFact: Wöhler made it from ammonium cyanate in 1828, proving organic molecules need no 'vital force'.

name: methylamine
funFact: Smells of rotting fish — amines are the smell of decay.

name: dimethyl sulfoxide
funFact: It passes straight through skin — you taste garlic seconds after touching it.

name: pyridine
funFact: The nitrogen lone pair points outward and is NOT part of the aromatic π system.

name: pyrrole
funFact: Here the N lone pair IS in the π system — two of the six aromatic electrons come from nitrogen.

name: purine
funFact: Adenine and guanine are both purines — fused six-and-five membered rings.

name: TNT
funFact: Remarkably stable — you can shoot a bullet through it; it needs a detonator to go off.

name: aspirin
funFact: Bayer patented it in 1899 — but willow bark was used for pain 3500 years earlier.

name: ibuprofen
funFact: It is sold as a racemate — only the S-enantiomer is active, but the body converts the R-form.

name: caffeine
funFact: It works by blocking adenosine receptors — your brain never gets the 'tired' signal.

name: nicotine
funFact: One of the most addictive alkaloids known — it mimics acetylcholine in the brain.

name: penicillin G
funFact: Fleming noticed it in 1928 because mould had killed the bacteria around it on a forgotten plate.

name: cholesterol
funFact: Every one of your cell membranes contains it — it stiffens the bilayer just enough.

name: glucose
funFact: In solution it spends 99.7% of its time in the ring form, not the open chain.

name: fructose
funFact: A structural isomer of glucose — same formula, a ketone instead of an aldehyde, and far sweeter.

name: sucrose
funFact: Glucose + fructose joined by an α,β-1,2-glycosidic bond — bees have been making it for 100 million years.

name: cellulose
funFact: The most abundant organic polymer on Earth — and humans cannot digest it.

name: starch
funFact: Same monomer as cellulose — the α linkage is why we can digest starch but not wood.

name: glycine
funFact: The only amino acid with no chiral centre — its side chain is just a hydrogen.

name: cysteine
funFact: Two cysteines oxidise to a disulfide bridge — the cross-link that holds your hair curls.

name: glutamic acid
funFact: Its sodium salt is monosodium glutamate — the original umami.

name: tryptophan
funFact: The turkey 'tryptophan coma' is a myth — the real culprit is the size of the meal.

name: adenine
funFact: Pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds in DNA.

name: guanine
funFact: Pairs with cytosine via THREE hydrogen bonds — GC-rich DNA is harder to unzip.

name: thymine
funFact: Thymine is just uracil with a methyl group — the '5-methyl' that stops DNA being mistaken for RNA.

name: ATP
funFact: You turn over roughly your own body weight in ATP every single day.

name: citric acid
funFact: The Krebs cycle is named after it — and it is what makes lemons sour.

name: lactic acid
funFact: The burn in your muscles is lactate, not lactic acid — the acid form appears at low pH.

name: oleic acid
funFact: The cis double bond puts a permanent kink in the chain — that is why olive oil is liquid.

name: vitamin C
funFact: Almost every mammal makes its own — humans, guinea pigs and fruit bats cannot.

name: vitamin A
funFact: The conjugated chain is exactly what lets retinal catch a photon and flip shape.

name: serotonin
funFact: About 90% of your serotonin is made in the gut, not the brain.

name: nitrate
funFact: All three N–O bonds are the same length — the double bond is delocalised.

name: hexacyanoferrate(III)
hazards: none — the cyanide is tightly bound
funFact: Prussian blue — the first modern synthetic pigment — is an iron hexacyanoferrate lattice.

name: tetraamminecopper(II)
funFact: Its intense azure blue is the classic test for copper(II) ions.

name: hexaamminecobalt(III)
funFact: Alfred Werner proved the octahedral geometry of complexes like this and won the 1913 Nobel Prize.
